title: The basilica
hook: early churches borrowed the Roman hall, a long nave to an apse

segments.voice: Yesterday, vows: a paper laid on an altar, poverty, chastity and obedience, or a Benedictine's stability. Your line was given wholly. Did your small vow last the whole day? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

The heavy door swings shut, and the traffic noise is gone. Ahead stretches a long, straight floor. Columns march down both sides in two rows, like trees along a country road. Light falls in from high windows. And far away, at the very end, the wall curves into a half-circle, glowing with gold mosaic, with an altar standing in front of it. There is only one direction this room wants anyone to go: forward. A whole church, shaped like a road. Today: the basilica.

Today the block turns from rites to spaces, and it starts with a building borrowed from Rome. First, the hall. Historians describe the Roman basilica as a big public building for law courts and business: a long central hall, columns down each side, and at the far end a rounded space called the apse, where an official sat to hear cases. Second, the choice. When Christians began building large churches, historians point out, they didn't copy the temples around them. A Roman temple was a house for a god's statue, and the crowd mostly stayed outside. Christian worship needed the crowd inside: everyone together, hearing the word and sharing the table. The public hall had room for that. Third, the change of furniture. The long central hall became the nave, where the people stand or sit. And at the far end, in the apse, where an official's seat had been, came the bishop's chair and, before it, the altar. A room built for judgment turned into a room built for worship, with a table at the end of the road. Fourth, the walk. The shape makes a path, door to altar, and people walk it. In processions. A bride up the aisle. People coming forward to receive communion. The psalms sing that movement: "Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise." And another: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD." The letter to the Hebrews uses the same picture for coming near to God: "boldness to enter into the holiest" by "a new and living way." Some churches built since, even ones that look nothing like Rome, still keep the long walk.
screen: `A ROMAN HALL FOR COURTS AND BUSINESS.`
`DOOR TO ALTAR: A PATH TO WALK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk slowly to the front of a church. If you can't get to one right now, walk it in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Start at the door. Feel it close behind you. Take one step on each slow breath. Notice the columns going by on either side, the light, the length of the floor. Don't hurry toward the end. Let the walk itself be the point. When you arrive, stand still at the front for a moment. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD. If you don't, simply stand there and look. The bell holds the time.
The basilica. A long Roman hall borrowed for worship: a nave for the people, an apse with the altar, and a path between them meant to be walked.

Your line: the long walk. This week went from go in peace, through for better, for worse, hands laid on, oil and prayer, we have left undone and given wholly, to the long walk. Today, walk somewhere slowly on purpose, and arrive. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Some churches, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, keep the basilica's long plan: a nave where the congregation gathers and a central aisle leading to the altar or communion table, walked in processions, at weddings and when people come forward to receive communion.

fork.setup: you're an early Christian community, ready to build a large church for the first time. your worship needs everyone inside, together. what do you build?

fork.reveal: historians say Christians borrowed the Roman basilica: a hall for crowds, with the official's seat at the end turned into the place of the altar.

trapdoor: what you thought: basilica just means a big, fancy church.
what it means: a long hall built for a crowd, nave to apse, with a walk to the altar at its heart.
what a scholar hears: historians trace the plan to Rome's public halls, where the official's seat in the apse gave way to the bishop's chair and the altar.

Architectural history (Roman basilica as a hall for courts and business; apse as the magistrate's seat; Christians choosing the hall over the temple form because worship gathered the crowd inside) is attributed to 'historians' and given without dates or names. A Keeper or historian should confirm; no specific text is cited for it.
'Many churches built since ... still keep the long walk' and howItsDone 'Many churches' are general; soften to 'some' if needed.
Fork option 'a small hidden room, like the houses you met in before' assumes house-church gatherings before large buildings; confirm the framing.
Original set to null: the Greek root of 'basilica' was left out under the etymology rule.
Hook's gold mosaic apse describes one imagined church, not every basilica.
